codes.platform: Harley-Davidson Twin Cam / Milwaukee-Eight EFI and Carbureted models (ECM), e.g. Dyna, Softail, Touring, Sportster
codes.description: Battery Voltage Low (ECM), also referred to in dealer documentation as "ECM voltage low" or "System Voltage Low". Per the Harley-Davidson Electrical Diagnostics Manual, DTC P0562 sets when battery voltage is less than 12.2 volts at idle and voltage does not increase when engine speed is greater than 2000 RPM. When P0562 or its high-voltage counterpart P0563 sets, the battery icon in the speedometer illuminates.
likely_causes: Charging system malfunction (failed stator or bad voltage regulator/rectifier) preventing voltage from rising above idle level
Loose, corroded, or high-resistance battery/ground connections
Weak or failing battery, or excessive battery draw / extended idling in heavy traffic causing voltage sag
TSSM/HFSM (security module) fault, which per the HD manual can also set P0562 or P0563
codes.first_check: Per Harley-Davidson's official Low/No Charging Diagnostics bulletin (M1507), the first step is to perform a battery test (load/charge test); if the battery passes, proceed to inspect and clean the main DC and AC charging-system connectors, then measure battery voltage with the engine running at 3,000 RPM to confirm it exceeds 13.8V before suspecting the stator or voltage regulator.
codes.confidence_note: Strong: verified against the actual quoted text of the 2008 Dyna Model Electrical Diagnostics Manual (via hdforums.com, a well-established Harley owner/technical forum whose thread reproduces the manual's exact detecting-condition and diagnostic-tip language), an official Harley-Davidson technical service bulletin (M1507, hosted by NHTSA) covering the same charging-system fault family on 2017-2023 Touring/Trike and 2018-2023 Softail platforms, and a second independent forum thread reproducing the identical manual language.

codes.platform: Harley-Davidson Twin Cam / Milwaukee-Eight EFI models with closed-loop fuel injection (Softail, Touring, Dyna, Sportster)
codes.description: Front Oxygen Sensor Low (also documented as "Front O2 sensor low (lean)" / "Front O2 sensor lean for any length of time"). Indicates the ECM has detected a persistently low-voltage (lean) signal from the front cylinder's oxygen sensor.
likely_causes: Exhaust air leak near the front oxygen sensor or head pipe (e.g., a cracked header or loose flange), which draws outside air past the sensor and reads falsely lean
An actual lean fuel condition on the front cylinder, most often from a plugged or failing front fuel injector
A misfire (ignition or fuel related) that increases oxygen content in the exhaust and mimics a lean signal, or a failing/degraded O2 sensor that can't produce its normal 0.0-1.0V signal range
Loose or improperly torqued O2 sensor, or damaged sensor wiring/connector causing high circuit resistance
codes.first_check: Inspect the exhaust system for leaks, starting at the front head pipe/flange bolts and the O2 sensor's mounting torque and seal; if no leak is found, check harness resistance between the ECM and front oxygen sensor connector for values indicating a ground short or open circuit (per the diagnostic manual procedure: resistance greater than 1 megohm indicates a sensor fault, requiring sensor replacement; lower resistance indicates a wiring short requiring harness repair).
codes.confidence_note: Strong: root causes and the code description are corroborated across three independent hdforums.com threads describing separate real-world cases (a cracked front header pipe, a stripped/loose O2 sensor, and general troubleshooting guidance), all reporting the same code name and consistent with standard closed-loop fuel-injection O2-sensor diagnostic logic. Note: the specific harness-resistance diagnostic procedure (1 megohm threshold) is drawn from a Subaru service-manual document found on Scribd describing an analogous P0131 O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage procedure -- it is NOT confirmed to be from a Harley-Davidson-specific manual, so it is presented here only as a representative generic O2-sensor-circuit diagnostic step, not as an HD-verified procedure. The Harley-specific 'first check' recommendation (exhaust leak inspection) is the one directly corroborated by Harley owner/technical sources.

codes.platform: Harley-Davidson carbureted models (2004 model year Softail, Touring, Dyna, Sportster) - Crankshaft Position (CKP) sensor circuit, per official Harley-Davidson Technical Service Bulletin M-1140
codes.description: Per Harley-Davidson Service Bulletin M-1140 ("EDM Update", issued October 8, 2003), the correct DTCs for the crank position sensor on carbureted models are P0371 (Crankshaft position shorted low / CKP sensor wrong number of pulses), P0372 (Crankshaft position shorted high), and P0374 (Crankshaft position sensor not detected / cannot synchronize). The bulletin explicitly corrected earlier 2004 diagnostic manuals that had incorrectly listed P0373 and P0374 for this fault; P0373 is stated as "not available." A DTC in this family sets if the CKP signal is weak, shorted, or absent.
codes.family: Sensor circuit (engine position / ignition timing reference)
likely_causes: Intermittent connection, pinched or damaged CKP sensor wiring, or a loose CKP sensor mounting fastener
Failed or degraded crankshaft position sensor unable to produce the minimum required AC signal (per the HD bulletin's diagnostic chart, at least 1 VAC during cranking) at its output terminals
Wiring shorted to ground or to voltage between the CKP sensor connector and the ignition control module (ICM)
codes.first_check: Per the official Harley-Davidson diagnostic flowchart in TSB M-1140, first check for intermittent connections, pinched/damaged wires, and a loose CKP sensor fastener; if none are found, connect a breakout box to the harness (leaving the ignition control module disconnected) and measure resistance between the CKP sensor terminals and ground -- resistance greater than 1 megohm is expected for a good circuit, with further AC-voltage cranking tests (minimum 1 VAC) used to isolate a bad sensor from a wiring fault.
codes.confidence_note: Strong: primary source is the actual scanned/hosted text of official Harley-Davidson Technical Service Bulletin M-1140 (an EDM/diagnostic-manual correction notice), independently corroborated by a separately-compiled dealer-sourced DTC reference document (hosted on S3, aggregating Harley diagnostic manuals) and further discussed by riders on an independent Harley owner forum reporting the same P0371/P0374 code pairing and description in the field.

codes.platform: Harley-Davidson ABS-equipped Touring and related models (front = C1032, rear = C1034)
codes.description: Wheel Speed Sensor Circuit Open or Shorted (Front or Rear). Per a Harley-Davidson electrical diagnostic manual excerpt reproduced by an owner, the DTC sets when the ABS module detects: a short to ground on either the high or low side circuit of the wheel speed sensor; an open on either the high or low side circuit; a short to voltage on the low side causing voltage above 0.79V; or the wheel speed sensor itself being open. When set, the ABS module disables ABS function and illuminates the ABS indicator.
likely_causes: A broken or pinched wheel speed sensor wire, commonly at the steering neck/fork area where the harness can stretch or rub when the handlebars are turned to full lock
Open circuit in either of the wheel speed sensor's high- or low-side wires, or a short to ground in the sensor wiring
A failed/open wheel speed sensor itself, or a short to battery voltage on the low-side circuit
codes.first_check: Per the Harley-Davidson diagnostic manual procedure, first inspect the wheel speed sensor wiring harness for physical damage (especially at the steering-neck/fork area for the front sensor), then use a breakout box / ohmmeter to check continuity between the ABS module connector and the wheel speed sensor connector; a broken or intermittent wire (frequently found at the neck where the harness contacts the frame at steering lock) is the most commonly reported real-world cause.
codes.confidence_note: Moderate-strong: the primary source is a hdforums.com thread that reproduces what its poster states is the verbatim Harley-Davidson diagnostic-manual page for 'DTC C1032, C1034: WHEEL SPEED SENSOR CIRCUIT OPEN OR SHORTED (FRONT OR REAR)', including specific tool part numbers (HD-41404-B, HD-48642) that support it being genuine dealer service literature rather than a paraphrase. This is independently corroborated by a second, separate hdforums.com thread describing a real-world C1032 case with a broken sensor wire at the steering neck as the root cause, and further supported contextually by an official NHTSA-hosted Harley-Davidson safety recall notice (Campaign 0175, RCMN-19V843-1027) confirming that faulty wheel-speed-sensor signals are a documented, safety-relevant fault class on Harley-Davidson ABS/traction-control-equipped motorcycles (Trike platform). IMPORTANT CAVEAT: an NHTSA-hosted bulletin literally titled 'M16-12-02 ABS Wheel Speed Sensor Diagnostics' with matching C1032/C1033/C1034/C1035 code numbers was initially found and looked like a strong third source, but on closer inspection it applies to the MV-1 wheelchair-accessible vehicle (Mobility Ventures LLC), NOT a Harley-Davidson motorcycle -- it was deliberately excluded from the sources list to avoid conflating an unrelated vehicle's identical-looking code numbers with Harley's own C-code family. Because full manufacturer PDF diagnostic-manual pages for C1032 could not be independently located on a second fully separate hosting source, this code is rated moderate-strong rather than fully verified against two wholly independent primary documents.
